overview.description: Sheepshead is a trick-taking game derived from Schafkopf and widely played in Wisconsin and other German-American communities. Standard play uses five players, a 32-card piquet deck, a two-card blind, and a hidden partner mechanic where the picker and partner try to reach 61 card points.
overview.deck: 32-card piquet deck (7, 8, 9, 10, J, Q, K, A in each suit)

history.origins: Sheepshead is the American descendant of Schafkopf, brought by German immigrants and adapted into regional U.S. rulesets.
timeline: 19th-20th century: German Schafkopf traditions spread to immigrant communities in the U.S.
20th century: Wisconsin and Midwest circles standardize local Sheepshead variants.
Present: Tournament and club play continues, with both in-person and online communities.
history.evolution: Regional variants developed around partner-calling, blind handling, and scoring multipliers while preserving the core trump hierarchy and trick-point counting.
history.cultural: Frequently played in Wisconsin social clubs and festivals, where it is often described as an unofficial state card game tradition.

setup.players: Standard game is five players with changing teams each hand; variants exist for 2-8 players.
setup.deck: Use a 32-card piquet deck (remove 2-6 from each suit in a standard deck).
setup.equipment: Cards and score tracking for game points.
setup.dealing: In the common five-player form, deal 6 cards to each player and 2 cards face down to the blind.

rules.objective: Picker side must take at least 61 of 120 card points; defenders win if picker side stays below 61.
rules.gameplay: After dealing, players may pass or pick the blind depending on table rules. The picker takes the blind, buries cards, and usually forms a hidden partnership (for example called-ace or jack-of-diamonds variants). Play is clockwise in tricks with mandatory suit following. Trump order is fixed with queens and jacks highest, plus diamonds as trumps in common five-player rules. After all tricks, card points determine whether picker side or defenders win.
keyRules: Players must follow suit when possible.
If trump is led and you hold trump, you must play trump.
Card points are counted from captured tricks; total points in hand are 120.

strategy.basic: Track trump strength and avoid wasting high trumps on low-point tricks.
strategy.intermediate: Count queens, jacks, and key point cards to infer whether picker side is ahead of the 61-point threshold.
strategy.advanced: Use lead control and hidden-partner inference to force opponents into point-losing trick lines.
tips: Point counting late in the hand is often more important than raw trick count.
When defending, pressure called-suit plays early to expose hidden partnerships.

list.description: Player holding jack of diamonds is partner; partnership remains hidden longer in many tables.

difficulty.medium: Tracks major trump cards and estimates card-point race around the 61-point threshold.
difficulty.hard: Performs partnership inference, point counting, and lead planning based on remaining trump density.

considerations: Hidden-partner inference from called-suit and smear behavior.
Dynamic team assignment and picker-role logic.
